sourceReviews.supportingSummary: I inspected the runtime-store description and the unit's T-SQL average-duration query, not just its heading. Runtime rows aggregate executions by plan and interval; the query divides SUM(rs.avg_duration * rs.count_executions) by NULLIF(SUM(rs.count_executions), 0) and explicitly uses floating-point arithmetic. This distinguishes an execution population from a population of row means. For the supplied complete nonoverlapping rows the denominator is 101. The report's Average/Maximum/Total alternatives support the other aggregation contexts; this is not evidence that the candidate was executed on SQL Server.

choiceReviews.rationale: The unit aggregates represented executions, not merely statistics rows. Giving the two means equal weight calculates (10 + 1000) / 2 = 505 even though their populations are 100 and 1. An equal-weight mean of interval means, or a fixture with equal execution counts, could justify AVG(avg_duration); neither describes these 101 executions.

Supported, not incorrect: the documented weighted calculation reconstructs 10*100 + 1000*1 = 2000 duration units and divides by 100 + 1 = 101 executions, approximately 19.801980198. The float means avoid integer division, counts are positive, and the stem excludes overlapping populations and mismatched units. These conditions make b the sole combined per-execution mean.

Multiplying each row mean by its count recovers represented duration, so this expression gives 2000, not a mean of 101 executions. It is appropriate for a summed-execution-duration question. The teaching formula contains this numerator but also the count denominator; omitting that denominator changes the requested metric.

The maximum supplied row mean is 1000. Selecting the worst interval mean is a legitimate Maximum-style comparison, but not the combined population mean. Nor does this expression generally reveal the slowest individual execution: its inputs are already averages. The unit’s runtime description and distinct report aggregations establish that boundary.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: I reread Understand deadlocks, Deadlock detection, Handle deadlocks, TRY...CATCH and the example contrasting explicit and autocommit transactions. Error 1205 follows termination and rollback of the victim transaction, not merely its last statement; the error instructs rerunning the transaction. Normal blocking instead waits for the owner to finish. The guide permits catching 1205 and recommends a brief randomized pause while warning that deadlocks cannot be completely avoided. Its autocommit example establishes when one statement can be an entire retry unit. None of this guarantees success or makes external business effects safe to replay.

choiceReviews.rationale: The guide makes the victim transaction the rollback unit. Here it contains both UPDATEs, so repeating only the second cannot restore the first one’s undone work. A failed autocommit statement that is itself the entire safe unit could be retried alone; the guide’s separate autocommit example illustrates that different boundary.

The 1205 handler runs after the original victim transaction was rolled back. No remaining original pair of updates exists for COMMIT to finalize. Committing a still-live, committable transaction after its work finishes is valid in the guide’s normal transaction-completion context, not after this victim rollback.

The raw guide distinguishes normal blocking from victim termination: a blocked transaction can continue when the lock owner finishes, but a 1205 victim cannot resume its discarded transaction. A randomized delay is useful before a new attempt; it does not revive the first UPDATE or the old transaction.

Supported, not incorrect: rerunning the entire victim transaction means beginning a new transaction and executing both updates again. The stem makes a bounded complete retry safe and excludes external side effects; the source recommends a randomized pause. This is a recovery strategy, not a promise of success on the next attempt.

reviews.verificationNotes: PASS 3 independently selects d. The strongest alternate interpretation is statement-only retry for a single autocommit operation; that fails the explicit two-statement victim here. I read the product’s transaction-wide rollback, normal-blocking contrast and TRY...CATCH text: a running CATCH does not prove a surviving transaction. Bounded safe retry and no external effects are supplied, and randomized delay does not guarantee success. No executable retry loop or SQL execution is claimed. SQL Server 2022 uses the ordinary GA victim mechanism; no service-tier, privileged diagnostic role, optimized-locking default or cheapest-victim shortcut is imported. Actual summary/document and root receipts were checked against existing DP-800 approvals. The SNAPSHOT neighbor needs rereading/recomputation; the sleeping-blocker neighbor concerns a still-live transaction. Rubric 46/48 deducts for easier distractor elimination and modest depth, including repeated complete-operation wording. No authored repair was made.
reviews.confidenceReason: High because the actual 1205 description rolls back the transaction and both UPDATEs are explicitly inside it. Supplied replay safety eliminates the external-effects ambiguity; approval does not endorse arbitrary operations or unbounded retry loops.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: I checked the actual Azure SQL Database vCore comparison, Compute, Data and log storage, Business Critical, Hyperscale and the high-vCore footnote. General Purpose and Business Critical have 4-TB data limits versus Hyperscale up to 128 TB, and Hyperscale supports named replicas for independent reads. Provisioned capacity is continuously allocated while serverless scales and bills for usage. The 160/192-vCore Preview footnote is real but unnecessary for the ordinary-GA-size scenario. These are SQL Database boundaries, not Managed Instance limits, universal default-tier advice or a guarantee that every SKU supports every maximum.

I read the separate service-tier and compute-tier sections. The unit matches provisioned compute to consistent demand and serverless to intermittent traffic, says serverless exists in General Purpose and Hyperscale, and separates compute choice from storage architecture. Its named-replica guidance supports read scale-out. I did not adopt broad unlimited-scaling, fixed-price-ratio or universal-latency prose: the candidate needs a finite 12-TB capacity comparison and a steady-workload recommendation.

choiceReviews.rationale: Provisioned compute fits the steady consumption, but General Purpose’s documented 4-TB data boundary is below the unsharded 12 TB required. A smaller moderate-I/O database with predictable demand can use General Purpose provisioned compute. Additional vCores do not change the service tier’s data-capacity boundary.

Business Critical offers local SSD and a readable secondary, so it could serve a smaller demanding OLTP/reporting workload. Its documented 4-TB data limit nevertheless fails this single 12-TB requirement. Better I/O and read offload are genuine capabilities, not substitutes for storage capacity.

General Purpose serverless retains General Purpose’s 4-TB limit. Serverless can suit an intermittent smaller database on supported hardware, but changing compute scaling cannot hold 12 TB. Steady demand favors provisioned compute; this is not a claim that serverless is technically unable to execute every steady workload.

Supported, not incorrect: documented Hyperscale capacity exceeds 12 TB and named replicas serve independent read scale-out. Provisioned compute matches steady demand. Available ordinary GA sizes are stipulated, so no Preview 160/192-vCore option is needed and no unlimited storage, optimal price, latency or immediate replica freshness is promised.

reviews.verificationNotes: PASS 3 independently selects d using 4 < 12 <= 128 TB, not a marketing default-tier label. Business Critical’s readable secondary and General Purpose’s serverless compute do not change their 4-TB data boundary. Sharding is excluded; region and ordinary GA sizes are supplied. Steady demand supports provisioned compute without making serverless impossible. Adjacent cache-policy and cross-domain metric/UDF questions require different facts. No authored field or source date was changed.

This does not attest production sizing, regional quota, actual price, performance or replica-consistency guarantees.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: I read all four database-configuration subsections. MAXDOP controls parallelism; FORCE_LAST_GOOD_PLAN corrects a query’s regression; compatibility level exposes optimizer behavior, with level 170 explicitly discussed; OPTIMIZE_FOR_AD_HOC_WORKLOADS has the shown ALTER DATABASE SCOPED CONFIGURATION syntax and retains a small compiled stub on first use instead of a full plan. Each option therefore has a different sourced useful context. I reject the unit’s broad assurance of important-plan residency: this candidate only targets first-use footprint, promises neither instant removal of old plans nor compilation avoidance, and is not a substitute for parameterization work.

choiceReviews.rationale: The unit describes MAXDOP as the parallel-execution control. Reducing it can be investigated for measured thread/CPU contention, but it does not select compiled stubs for first-use ad hoc entries. The supplied diagnosis concerns retained cache storage, not excessive parallel execution.

Supported, not incorrect: the raw unit gives the database-scoped OPTIMIZE_FOR_AD_HOC_WORKLOADS switch and explains that first use retains a small compiled stub rather than the full plan. That matches the storage objective. It is not proof of compilation avoidance, retroactive old-plan eviction or permanent residency of reused plans.

Compatibility level 170 is a real Azure SQL Database optimizer-behavior choice in the unit. Testing a newer optimizer feature against a baseline can justify that change. It does not specify first-use compiled-stub retention, so optimizer modernization is not the requested cache-policy control.

FORCE_LAST_GOOD_PLAN addresses a query that regresses to a worse plan and has a better earlier plan to restore. The stem instead describes many distinct statements used once occupying cache. Correcting one query’s regression does not establish a first-use stub-retention policy.

reviews.verificationNotes: PASS 3 independently selects b after reading all four actual configuration sections and testing their alternative diagnoses.
